title: In Odesa, no-one is safe from Russia's new Black Sea strike campaign
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Russian missiles and drones are hammering Ukraine's Black Sea ports, like OdesaByPaul AdamsDiplomatic corresp
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Russian missiles and drones are hammering Ukraine's Black Sea ports, like OdesaByPaul AdamsDiplomatic correspondent in Odesa"My crane operator, my partner, died five metres from me… The driver remained in the cabin. He also died."Svitlana Halchenko winces as she remembers the Russian ballistic missile which exploded at work in Odesa, killing her colleagues. Svitlana works as a warehouse shift manager at the city's main port.Despite her injuries – she walks with a limp, pieces of shrapnel still embedded in her leg and back – Svitlana is determined to keep working.But her normally bustling workplace is largely silent.Russia is ramping up its efforts to strangle Ukraine's commercial links to the outside world, launching attacks all along the country's Black Sea coastline.From damaged port infrastructure to listing ships with bridges blackened and containers still smouldering, the evidence is everywhere. Nowhere more so than out towards the horizon, where the approaches to Ukraine's once bustling ports – Odesa, Chornomorsk, Pivdennyi – are almost devoid of ships.See more of Paul Adams' trip to Odesa here on YouTube, externalSvitlana maintains a brave smile throughout our conversation, but her distress is painfully obvious. Her fingers constantly twist a tissue as she tries to maintain her composure and she gazes into the distance as tears well up behind her glasses.The last few weeks have been worse than ever."It's been very difficult for morale," she says with a deep sigh. "A lot of sirens, a lot of shaheds [drones], a lot of hits. People are very tense."Maarten Lernout/BBCMy crane operator, my partner, died five metres from me… The driver remained in the cabin. He also diedAccording to Ukraine's port administration, July saw 57 Russian attacks on civilian vessels, 22 of them at sea, and a further 67 hits on port infrastructure.While there have been Russian attacks on international vessels before, they've never been so numerous or so deadly.On July 19, a Turkish-owned cargo vessel, Golden Leo, was struck by three Russian missiles, killing nine Indian and Syrian crew members and a Ukrainian pilot.The ship, carrying Ukrainian corn, sank off Odesa a week later.According to the global shipping journal Lloyd's List, the Black Sea may now be the most dangerous place for shipping in the world - with July the deadliest month for merchant seamen, external since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began. At his union's offices in the port city, Oleg Grygoriuk, Chairman of the Marine Transport Workers Union of Ukraine, says his members are suffering."There are a lot of veterans who already served their country," he says, "and they literally say that being in the port is more scary than being on the front line."Odesa's proximity to Russian-occupied territory means that workers often have little time to react."A missile flies from Crimea within a minute," he says. "If you are sitting in a crane, you need three and a half minutes to get down and go to the shelter. There's literally no time to do that."On a rare visit to one of the area's main ports, we saw almost no sign of movement. Hundreds of metres of berths sat empty and towering gantry cranes stood idle as a skeleton crew conducted maintenance.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Odesa's port lies empty now as Russia steps up its attacksThe military authorities allowed the visit on strict condition that we neither name the facility nor film anything. Ukraine doesn't want Russia to know what has and hasn't been damaged or reveal details that might aid Moscow in further targeting.Two damaged cargo vessels were moored nearby. Both had suffered severe damage to the superstructure, where the bridge and crew quarters are located.Just one lone freighter was seen moving towards the port."My heart is broken," a senior manager told us on condition we didn't name him."Normally there's a queue, even out at sea, waiting for a berth.""There was a deal," he said, referring to the UN-brokered 2022 Black Sea Grain Initiative, under which Russia agreed to lift its blockade on Ukraine's agricultural exports. The agreement established safe maritime corridors to Odesa's main ports."They stopped the deal in the middle of 2023, but they didn't start attacking it until recently," the manager said."Today they do it systematically."Halfway through our tour, sirens sounded, forcing us to seek shelter for several minutes as a Russian jet-powered drone flew overhead.Weary dock workers scanned their phones for updates until the all-clear sounded.The manager said recent alerts have forced the port to shut down for 15 out of 24 hours.Technically, the port is open, as are all the others in the area. There is no prohibition on commercial ships attempting to use them. But the risks are clearly too great for most shipowners."There is barely anybody who wants to call because there is a huge problem with people getting killed," says Andrey Stavnitser, co-owner and CEO of one of the largest ports in the area."We can see that the whole supply chain is on hold."Image caption, Russia has made Ukraine's Black Sea coastline incredibly dangerous for shippingStavnitser says Russia is almost certainly retaliating for Ukraine's recent, highly successful attacks on Russian shipping, including sanctioned vessels carrying oil, as well as other ships involved in ferrying supplies to Russian-occupied Crimea.Using its own drones, Ukraine's Operation MoLoChKa (which roughly translates as "Moscow will fall through Crimea") has struck around 200 Russian vessels, bringing traffic in the strategic Sea of Azov to a virtual standstill.Ukrainians bristle at the suggestion that Russia and Ukraine are playing the same game. Kyiv is attempting to loosen Moscow's grip on occupied territory, they point out, while Russia is preventing Ukraine from exporting badly needed grain to the international market.With Ukraine's summer grain harvest well under way, this is all happening at the worst possible time."It's the most sensitive period," says Volodymyr Slavinskyi, trading director for Nibulon, one of the country's leading grain exporters."Farmers need to quickly harvest grains from the fields, not to lose the crop. They need to be able to sell the crop they harvested and reinvest money in the next production cycle."The impact of a prolonged shutdown of Ukraine's ports are likely to be severe. Ukraine is one of the world's largest producers of grain and oilseeds, supplying around 6% of global wheat exports before Russia's full-scale invasion and 10% of corn exports. But reports suggest, external its export capacity has dropped by at least a third since Russia launched its full-scale invasion.The Black Sea remains a vital export route for the country. Last year, the Greater Odesa ports accounted for more than 73 million tonnes of Ukraine's maritime exports, with grain accounting for 38 million tonnes.With almost no vessels currently moving on Ukraine's Black Sea shipping corridor, traders are already counting the cost of this summer's closure."I would say we've already lost the ability to deliver to global customers around half a million or 700,000 metric tons of Ukrainian grains and oilseeds," Slavinskyi says.Image source, Kristina Volk/BBCImage caption, Volodymyr Slavinskyi says Ukraine has lost a huge amount of its export capacityAway from the port, Odesa is determined to show off a very different side. The summer season is in full swing. The beaches are packed as visitors descend on the Black Sea from all over Ukraine.Buskers perform on the city's famous Potemkin Stairs, while sunbathers barely flinch as the sirens sound and explosions rumble in the distance.In a video published on Monday, swimmers were seen removing a Russian drone from the water as holidaymakers look on.They know the risks. In late June, 26-year-old Daria Kravchenko was killed when shrapnel from an intercepted Russian drone landed on the beach.This week, holidaymakers on Russia's equally Black Sea coast suffered a similar fate when an intercepted Ukrainian drone crashed onto a busy beach.Local authorities said seven people were killed, including three children.It's not clear what Ukraine was targeting, but this war on ships and ports has many casual victims. Sailors, dockworkers or people simply unlucky enough to live or work nearby.Outside Odesa, after a recent drone explosion, we found 83-year-old Andrii Dudik, surveying the mangled wreckage of his house and garden.He was physically unscathed and remarkably sanguine about the drone that had shattered his routine afternoon nap just hours earlier."I was lying there, wondering what I was going to do this afternoon. Now I know," he joked.Did he feel like an accidental victim of Russia's attacks on the nearby ports, I asked him."Absolutely," he replied. "And I won't forget it."Additional reporting by Kristina Volk, Anastasiia Levchenko, Volodymyr Lozhko and Joshua Cheetham

title: Supreme Court on walking: India is a nation of walkers - but its cities forgot them
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Around 45 million people walk to work every day, according to census-based estimatesByIndia correspon
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Around 45 million people walk to work every day, according to census-based estimatesByIndia correspondentFor much of my life, walking in Indian cities has felt less like exercising a right than negotiating an obstacle course.I grew up in Kolkata, where wide pavements disappeared beneath rows of hawkers. I moved to Delhi, where roads seemed designed almost exclusively for cars. Now I live in Gurugram, where footpaths vanish into rubble and garbage, are abruptly blocked by parked vehicles or construction, or sit uncomfortably high above the road.So when India's Supreme Court declared in June that the right to walk safely on designated footpaths was a fundamental right, external, it felt less like judicial activism than common sense arriving decades late.Walking is the most democratic form of transport. Yet it is also the one India's cities have neglected most consistently.It's remarkable because India remains, above all, a nation of walkers. Around 45 million people walk to work every day, according to census-based estimates, compared with only about 5.4 million who commute in private cars, jeeps or vans.Nearly a third of urban workers walk to work, while virtually every bus or metro journey begins and ends on foot. Add school runs, shopping trips and other everyday journeys, and walking dominates urban mobility. A 2019 survey of selected cities found that 63% of all journeys were made on foot, making pedestrians the single largest group of road users.Many are what researchers call "captive pedestrians" - people who walk not by choice but because they cannot afford another option. Women are especially dependent on walking. Yet the people who contribute least to congestion and pollution often face the greatest risks.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, A woman walks past poles and wires strewn across a footpath in ChennaiThe evidence is harrowing. Even where pavements exist, they are often broken, narrow or inaccessible to older people, children and those with disabilities.They are also blocked by motorcycles, swallowed by parked cars, encroachments or excavated for utility works. Faded zebra crossings are treated as little more than road markings no-one respects. Flyovers speed traffic while forcing pedestrians into hazardous detours below. A landmark 2011 study of six Indian cities found that India's streets routinely fail pedestrians because of "poor and unsafe" infrastructure.The Walkability in Indian Cities report by the Clean Air Initiative for Asian Cities (CAI-Asia) gave the surveyed cities a median walkability score of just 47 out of 100, with the worst conditions around public transport terminals - ironically the places where most journeys begin and end on footAs Geetam Tiwari, a transport scholar at Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi puts it, pedestrians have been "pushed to the margins of the road networks" forcing them to "jostle for space with motor vehicles".The price is paid in lives.Officially pedestrians account for roughly a fifth of road deaths, external, but independent studies cited by Tiwari estimate the share is closer to 30-40%.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Motorcyclists riding on a pedestrian footpath along a bridge in DelhiPedestrians are also the second-largest group of road accident victims after two-wheeler riders. In Delhi and Mumbai, they account for more than half of all road deaths. According to a World Bank study, crashes already cost India an estimated 3-5% of its GDP each year through lost productivity, healthcare costs and disability.The Supreme Court case arose from one such tragedy: a five-year-old boy crushed by a truck while walking to school with his father.The judges responded with unusual eloquence. Walking, Justice PS Narasimha wrote, is "the simplest of the simple human activity, inextricably connected to life". Roads therefore impose a corresponding duty on the state to provide safe footpaths. "The fundamental right to walk on demarcated footpaths shall override the privilege of a motorised vehicle," he declared.The judgment challenges decades of Indian urban planning, where progress has often been measured in kilometres of expressways, flyovers and elevated corridors. Streets were engineered to move vehicles as quickly as possible, while the one road user every citizen inevitably becomes - the pedestrian - largely disappeared from planners' imagination."People know about the latest cars, but walking has become invisible," says Rishi Aggarwal, who has spent more than a decade trying to change that mindset in Mumbai.Through city walks and public talks, his advocacy group, Walking Project, encourages residents to notice what they have stopped seeing: broken pavements, blocked crossings and unsafe junctions - and compare them with the standards pedestrians are entitled to expect. "When people become apathetic, they stop observing the street," he says.Image source, NurPhoto via Getty ImagesImage caption, Zebra crossings - like this one in Kolkata - are treated as little more than road markings In a city where an estimated 15 million walking trips are made every day, Aggarwal argues, it is not just footpaths that have disappeared from view, but also the millions of people who depend on them.For Rahul Goel, a transportation researcher at Delhi's Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), the problem begins with governance. "Are footpaths maintained and cleaned? Does the city ensure they aren't encroached upon?" he says. "In Delhi, many roads do have footpaths, but they're often unusable because of poor governance."Poor design makes matters worse. Cars parked perpendicular to the kerb often conceal footpaths or block them altogether, while vehicles parked directly on pavements are a common sight. Footpaths are often too narrow for the number of pedestrians. Many are so high above the road that older people, wheelchair users and others with limited mobility struggle to use them. Others end abruptly, forcing people back onto the carriageway."If the footpath is discontinuous, it's simply more convenient to keep walking on the road," says Goel.He believes the deeper problem is one of priorities. "Urban transport governance is still centred on moving vehicles. Reducing congestion and maximising road space for motor traffic take precedence over pedestrians," he says. Civic agencies are often reluctant to widen footpaths because they view carriageway space as sacrosanct. That mindset, Goel argues, is reinforced by public pressure. Image source, NurPhoto via Getty ImagesImage caption, A pedestrian walks through a haze of dust pollution in HyderabadTraffic jams dominate headlines and social media, pushing authorities to keep vehicles moving. In Delhi, many mid-block crossings have been replaced by U-turns to reduce stoppages, forcing pedestrians onto foot overbridges. "People don't just need to walk along a road," says Goel. "They need to be able to cross it safely too."The result is a stark urban inequality. In Gurugram, a high-speed arterial road cuts through busy neighbourhoods with few safe crossings. Domestic workers, labourers and other pedestrians routinely dodge speeding traffic, and many are killed trying to cross. Only after the death toll mounted did authorities begin building footbridges.Across India's cities, those who cannot afford cars or motorcycles are left to risk their lives on roads that barely accommodate pedestrians. Those who can drive claim an ever-larger share of public space, while walking becomes a leisure activity confined to gated communities, parks or gym treadmills. In a country grappling with rising obesity and lifestyle diseases, cities have turned the most basic form of exercise into something not just inconvenient, but too often dangerous.Clearly, making people walk will require far more than a court order."Walking as a fundamental right should lead to pedestrian-friendly cities, not just pedestrian-friendly streets," says Tiwari.That means rethinking how cities are designed. Some countries have adopted default urban speed limits of 30km/h or 20mph to protect pedestrians, regardless of the type of road. Achieving that, Tiwari says, requires redesigning streets by narrowing traffic lanes, altering road surfaces and introducing other traffic-calming measures. Image source, NurPhoto via Getty ImagesImage caption, A man with a physical disability navigates a busy road in KolkataThe judges also reflected on walking as something far greater than a way of getting from one place to another. It can be "necessity for the poor, meditation for some, an act of resistance for others and a path to discovery. Walking, they noted, also helped shape India's freedom struggle".As writer Sumana Roy notes, external, India's political history has often unfolded on foot -from Gandhi's "salt march" to Dandi to Subhas Chandra Bose's "Delhi Chalo" (March to Delhi) and the many protest marches that followed.For Tiwari, that broader understanding of walking should also shape how cities are built. "Walking is more than a travel option," she says. "Therefore a safe walking infrastructure requires more than creating footpaths and safe crossing. Walking spaces have to integrate activities like spaces of street vendors, shaded paths, areas for resting for old people and sometimes space where children can play."For decades, Indian cities have asked how to move more vehicles. The top court has reminded them to ask a simpler one: how do people walk?I'd settle for something wonderfully unremarkable: a footpath that simply carries me from one end of the street to the other.

schema.headline: Supreme Court on walking: India is a nation of walkers - but its cities forgot them

title: Gianni Infantino: Uefa says Fifa's backing of its president 'changes nothing'
description: European teams could still boycott competitions including the World Cup as Uefa says Fifa's defence of its president Gianni Infantino "changes nothing
body: European teams could still boycott competitions including the World Cup as Uefa says Fifa's defence of its president Gianni Infantino "changes nothing".The English FA has sent a letter withdrawing its support for Infantino in reaction to the plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.European governing body Uefa said in a statement its conditions had not been met, despite Infantino's plan being aborted."First, the proposals to sell off the major competitions had to be withdrawn and secondly," Uefa's statement said. "Assurances have to be made that such attempts to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again."These conditions have not been met."Uefa has already said it has lost confidence in Infantino, calling the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal a "shabby, back room, opaque deal".But on Thursday, Conmebol, the South American confederation, and the Confederation of African Football (Caf) backed Infantino, as did the football associations of World Cup co-hosts Mexico and tournament runners-up Argentina.Infantino had offered all associations $40m (£30m) if they backed a proposal for private investment in its tournaments, including the men's and women's World Cups, through the FFE subsidiary.World governing body Fifa said during Wednesday's meeting "mistakes" regarding FFE were "acknowledged", saying it was "not the intention" for the Fifa Council and members association to "feel excluded from the process and that the process should have been handled differently".Uefa's statement in response added: "Uefa made it abundantly clear in its statement on Saturday that it has lost confidence in Gianni Infantino's presidency. That position holds."Yesterday's announcement that some people employed by the Fifa president (and whose careers depend on his favour) agree with him changes nothing."Fifa has been approached for comment.Infantino arrived at Fifa's offices in Rabat, Morocco on Wednesday in now-familiar fashion, chauffeured to the building in a motorcade, sitting in the back of a Mercedes with blacked out windows.Some questioned whether he would still be the Fifa president when he left.Yet if anything, on the surface at least, Infantino appears emboldened.This was not the 56-year-old being ordered to a hearing to explain his actions. It was Infantino who summoned members of the Fifa management board to sit around the table with him, to talk through the events of the last week.Secretary general Mattias Grafstrom, Infantino's right-hand man, had been critical in an internal memo to staff, calling the FFE proposals "a sad and reproachable series of events".After the meeting finished it appeared to be water under the bridge, with Infantino and Grafstrom pictured sat next to each other and smiling at a Women's Africa Cup of Nations match between Malawi and Zambia. If there were clear-the-air talks, they appear to have worked. Other members of the Fifa management board to attend the meeting included finance chief Thomas Peyer, legal chief Emilio Garcia Silvero, chief of staff Daniel O'Toole, chief of member associations Elkhan Mammadov and media relations director Bryan Swanson.BBC Sport has been told that Fifa's chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, was not invited.Lamour strongly criticised Infantino's FFE plan, saying it was "the project of one person", and "the time has now come for football's political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions". He added: "I lose my job, then so be it. At least I'll sleep well tonight."Lamour has declined to comment to the BBC. Fifa has been approached for comment.What concerns Uefa is that this meeting was a gathering of employees who are themselves part of the regime. It is unknown if Infantino was forced to answer difficult questions about his plan. Questions such as: who was involved? Whether there was a competitive tender process? And if he stood to benefit personally? While Fifa said "mistakes made were acknowledged" and an "apology was made", there was no direct accountability for the controversy.Uefa still wants answers to those key questions and will not be content until it gets them - or Infantino leaves.Uefa is in something of a pickle as it tries to get rid of Infantino.The easiest route to success was the slow turning of the vice throughout this week, hoping to exert enough pressure to force him to quit.Yet the Swiss appears to have no intention of walking away.European football looks like an outlier, struggling to gain enough support to topple him. On Thursday, Lamin Kaba Bajo, the president of the Gambia Football Federation, praised Infantino's "courage" and for the U-turn, and said he was "willing to give him my support more than ever".Only Jordan, one of the few countries which did not back Infantino before last week, has publicly stated it will not vote for his re-election in March. Concacaf, which oversees football in North and Central America and the Caribbean, also issued a public statement after the proposal was aborted but, unlike Uefa, it did not go as far as to say it had lost confidence in the Fifa president. Conmebol said on Thursday it would not support "any action or procedure that disregards" Fifa's mechanisms before the presidential election. Similarly, the Mexican Football Federation shared a statement to X expressing their support for Infantino, saying it would not recognise or approve any process convened outside of Fifa's institutional framework. The Argentine Football Association also published a letter in support of Infantino and the Fifa board, which it said had provided "institutional solidity" with its current "stable and transparent" business model.Caf said its executive committee "unanimously reconfirmed" its support for Infantino and thanked him for his support for African football over the years.Ideally, Uefa would force an emergency meeting of the Fifa Council, to provide what it would consider to be a true chance to hold Infantino to account.But getting the necessary 19 of 36 confederation and football association heads to support it has proven to be exceptionally difficult. Uefa has also kept on the table the option of a vote of no confidence, which it can trigger via an extraordinary congress any time it wishes. However, it would need a majority of Fifa's 211 member associations - 106 votes - to pass the motion. It would be a de facto presidential election without a second candidate. If Uefa does not think it can get to 106, which looks a stretch, then there is little point in triggering the vote. The other option is to try to find a unity candidate to stand against Infantino in the election next March. The favourite would be Concacaf president Victor Montagliani. Any option which takes time gives Infantino space to build bridges, and with Fifa due to announce new funding to member associations by the end of the year he could dangle another carrot for his re-election.  Unless Uefa sticks by the nuclear option - and goes through with its threat of a boycott.This has issues, and it is not a lever you can pull very often, otherwise it gives the impression of riding roughshod over the rest of the world.It is one thing to use it to jettison the FFE proposal, another entirely to effectively dethrone the president with it. Uefa's stance will soon be tested, with the Fifa Women's U20s World Cup kicking off in Poland on 5 September. Six European countries are due to take part, including England. Some at the European confederation claim Wednesday's statement shows exactly why the beleaguered president must step down.The feeling within Uefa is that the statement was far from representative of the entire world governing body, and that there has been a lack of consultation with the council or membership.There is also a view that Infantino is trying to swerve personal responsibility by sharing out the blame for the aborted proposals, and that he alone should have apologised - rather than issue his expression of regret alongside his deputy Grafstrom.In stark contrast, within Fifa, the view from one Infantino loyalist is that the outcry, especially in Europe, is bordering on "hysteria", and fails to acknowledge the legitimacy he has globally.By clinging to power, Infantino has mounted the start of an attempted fightback. But it could yet fuel the revolt against him, both from outside and within Fifa. And it looks increasingly likely his opponents will have to identity the rival candidate that could challenge him at next year's presidential election.
